paras: The threatened lynching near Franklin, Tennessee, in 1888 was a reported threat against an unnamed Black man said to have tried to stop the buggy horse of two young women outside the town. The women escaped, and a brief published on 22 November 1888 said the man would be lynched if caught, but no capture or lynching was reported.

According to the Clarksville Evening Chronicle, Miss Mary Nichol and Miss Leela Vaughn were driving in a buggy near Franklin when "a colored man attempted to stop their horse." The horse was whipped, and the buggy wheel threw the man down as the two women got away. The item gives no date for the encounter, names no witnesses beyond the two women, and does not say what the man intended.

The brief closed with the statement that "the negro will be lynched if caught and indicted," without naming any group making the threat. No report of an arrest, a search, a lynching or any court proceeding appears in the coverage.

The only known account ran without a headline on page 3 of the Clarksville Evening Chronicle, in a column of national news briefs titled "Pointed Paragraphs" and subtitled "Topics of the Times Given in a Terse and Spicy Manner." It sat between an item on a suicide at Pittsburg and a dispatch on a vessel fire at Sandusky, Ohio, and it called the man "a colored man" and then "the negro." The paper presented the coming lynching as a matter of course rather than as something to report or condemn, and it gave only the women's side of the encounter.
